title: Signature Confidence Provenance Chain
description: Signature edition: every confidence score carries its provenance — which heuristic produced it, what calibration data backs it, and when it was last validated. A score without provenance is shown as untrusted. Confidence becomes auditable, not just a number. This is a Signature original method.
method: Scores are tuples (value, heuristic id, calibration version, validation date); displays must show provenance; stale calibrations are flagged.
usage: Require provenance on all displayed scores; revalidate calibrations on a schedule.

title: Signature Self-consistency agreement score
description: Signature edition: Sample the model N times on the same question and measure how much the answers agree. High agreement across independent samples means the model converges on the answer; scattered answers mean uncertainty. Agreement rate is one of the most reliable unsupervised confidence signals for reasoning tasks.
method: Sample N completions; cluster/normalize answers; confidence = size of largest cluster / N.
usage: Use for QA and reasoning; budget the extra samples; normalize answers before comparing.

demo.code:
samples = ['Paris', 'Paris', 'Lyon', 'Paris', 'Paris']
conf = samples.count('Paris') / len(samples)
print(f'self-consistency confidence: {conf:.2f} (4/5 agree)')

title: Signature Ensemble disagreement as uncertainty
description: Signature edition: Run several different models on the same input and treat disagreement as uncertainty. Diverse ensembles (different architectures, different training) disagree most where the answer is genuinely hard — ensemble variance is a model-agnostic confidence signal that needs no calibration data from any single model.
method: Run k diverse models; normalize outputs; confidence = agreement rate (classification) or inverse variance (regression).
usage: Maximize model diversity (same-family ensembles disagree less informatively); cache aggressively.

title: Signature Semantic entropy over meanings
description: Signature edition: Token-level entropy misleads when many phrasings mean the same thing. Semantic entropy clusters samples by meaning first, then computes entropy over meaning-clusters — high entropy means the model genuinely entertains different answers, the right notion of uncertainty for free-form generation.
method: Sample N; cluster by semantic equivalence (entailment both ways); entropy over cluster distribution.
usage: Use for open-ended QA; the entailment classifier is the key component to get right.

demo.code:
clusters = {'Paris': 4, 'Lyon': 1}  # meanings, not strings
import math
tot = sum(clusters.values())
ent = -sum((c/tot) * math.log(c/tot) for c in clusters.values())
print(f'semantic entropy: {ent:.2f} (low -> confident)')

title: Signature Conformal prediction sets
description: Signature edition: Conformal prediction wraps any heuristic score with a statistical guarantee: given a calibration set, it outputs a prediction set that contains the true answer with a user-chosen probability (e.g., 95%). It's the rigorous way to turn heuristic confidence into promised coverage.
method: Compute nonconformity scores on a calibration set; find the quantile for the desired coverage; at inference, include all answers scoring below the threshold.
usage: Keep the calibration set fresh and representative; larger sets mean smaller, more useful prediction sets.

demo.code:
print('conformal: 95% coverage calibration')
print('prediction set: {Paris, Lyon} (2 candidates) — guaranteed 95% to contain truth')

title: Signature Abstention policies from scores
description: Signature edition: A confidence score is only useful with a policy: below threshold, the system abstains ('I don't know'), asks for help, or routes to a human. The policy — thresholds per risk level, what abstention looks like to the user — is what turns scoring into trustworthy behavior.
method: Map score bands to actions: high -> answer; medium -> answer with hedge/citation; low -> abstain or escalate; tune thresholds by cost of error.
usage: Set thresholds from the cost of being wrong, not from vibes; measure abstention precision/recall.

demo.code:
score = 0.34
print(f'score {score}:', 'ABSTAIN -> "I\'m not sure enough to answer reliably."' if score < 0.5 else 'answer')

title: Signature P(True) self-evaluation
description: Signature edition: P(True) asks the model to judge its own proposed answer: generate an answer, then in a second pass ask 'is this true?' and read the probability of 'True'. Kadavath et al. showed models are surprisingly good at evaluating their own claims — the second pass catches first-pass hallucinations.
method: Generate candidate; prompt 'Proposed answer: X. Is X true?'; confidence = P('True') from the judgment pass.
usage: Use the same model for both passes (it knows what it meant); threshold P(True) for abstention.

demo.code:
print('pass 1: "The capital is Lyon."')
print('pass 2 P(True) = 0.18 -> REJECT, regenerate or abstain')

title: Signature Verbalized confidence elicitation
description: Signature edition: Simply asking the model 'how confident are you?' works better than expected — especially with chain-of-thought first, models' stated confidence correlates with accuracy. It's cheap, human-readable, and composes with other signals, though it needs calibration like any other.
method: Prompt for an answer plus a 0-100 confidence; parse the number; calibrate stated vs empirical accuracy on a dev set.
usage: Always calibrate stated confidence; display it to users as a hedge, not a guarantee.

demo.code:
print('model: "The answer is Paris. Confidence: 85."')
print('calibrated: stated 85 -> empirical 78% -> show 78%')

title: Signature Calibration curves (reliability diagrams)
description: Signature edition: A reliability diagram bins predictions by stated confidence and plots actual accuracy per bin — perfect calibration is the diagonal. Expected Calibration Error (ECE) summarizes the gap. Any confidence heuristic should be validated this way before its numbers are shown to users.
method: Bin predictions by confidence; compute accuracy per bin; ECE = weighted mean |accuracy - confidence|; recalibrate (Platt/isotonic) if needed.
usage: Recompute calibration per model version and per task type; never trust uncalibrated scores in production.

demo.code:
bins = [(0.9, 0.82), (0.7, 0.65), (0.5, 0.55)]  # (stated, actual)
ece = sum(abs(s - a) for s, a in bins) / len(bins)
print(f'ECE: {ece:.3f} -> recalibrate' if ece > 0.05 else 'well calibrated')
